articles.title: Burns and scalds
articles.summary: Recognising when a burn needs prompt assistance and preparing a first-aid response.

sections.title: Recognise the situation
paragraphs: Burns and scalds can result from heat, hot liquids, chemicals, electricity or radiation. The cause and seriousness affect what care is appropriate. This article is an editorial draft, not a clinical assessment.

Pay attention to warning signs such as large or deep injury, breathing problems, a burn involving an infant or vulnerable person, or a possible electrical or chemical cause. These situations may require urgent professional help.

sections.title: General first-aid planning
paragraphs: Keep accessible contact information, a well-stocked first-aid kit and the location of the nearest appropriate medical service in your household plan.

Seek up-to-date professional first-aid guidance for cooling, covering and escalation. Do not put ice, greasy products or unverified home remedies on an injured area; inappropriate treatments can make injury worse.

sections.title: When to seek help
paragraphs: Use emergency services for severe injury, difficulty breathing, or other signs of immediate danger. In the UK, 999 and 112 are emergency numbers. For non-emergency medical assessment, use the locally applicable health service.
A small-looking burn may still need assessment depending on cause, depth, location and the person affected. This draft cannot distinguish safe home management from injuries requiring treatment.

sections.title: Related supplies and source status
paragraphs: A first-aid kit, working phone, emergency contacts and access to drinking water may be useful preparedness items, but they do not substitute for training.
This entry has not been clinically reviewed. A medical professional should approve the final wording and any instructional illustrations before it is released as a public safety guide.

articles.title: Damaged electrical cable
articles.summary: Identify warning signs and choose safer next steps rather than attempting risky cable repairs.

sections.title: Signs that a cable needs attention
paragraphs: Cracked insulation, exposed wires, scorch marks, unusual heat, damaged plug casings or intermittent operation may indicate an electrical problem. Electrical faults can present fire and shock risks.
A cable can appear intact while still being unsuitable for use; visual inspection alone cannot establish safety.

sections.title: Avoid improvised repairs
paragraphs: Do not treat tape, glue or a makeshift splice as a safe repair to a mains cable. Keep people from using equipment known or suspected to be damaged and follow manufacturer instructions.
If there is smoke, arcing, burning smell, water exposure or immediate danger, prioritise personal safety and seek emergency or qualified help. Do not handle an energised, damaged cable.

sections.title: Repair or replacement decision
paragraphs: For mains wiring, fixed installations and uncertainty about electrical safety, use a competent electrician. For replaceable equipment leads, consult the manufacturer or an appropriately qualified professional about compatible replacement.
This library does not provide instructions for stripping, joining, rewiring or energising mains conductors, because incorrect work can cause serious injury or fire.

sections.title: Household record
paragraphs: Note the device and its location, label it as needing attention and record the relevant manufacturer or electrician contact. Do not mark the task complete simply because a cable has been visually inspected.
This article is a general preparedness draft; UK electrical standards, product requirements and any repair procedures require qualified verification.

articles.title: Cuts and minor wounds
articles.summary: First-aid kit planning, basic hygiene and reasons to seek medical assessment.

sections.title: Assess before acting
paragraphs: Minor cuts and more serious wounds can look similar at first. Heavy bleeding, deep wounds, loss of sensation, contamination or injury to a child may require urgent assessment.
A first-aid kit is useful only when people know where it is and how to use its contents safely.

sections.title: Prepare suitable materials
paragraphs: Record clean dressings, plasters, gloves and any other appropriate materials in the household inventory. Replace opened, wet or damaged items where necessary.
Keep a clear plan for getting medical help and for relevant individual needs such as medicine allergies or treatment considerations.

sections.title: After initial care
paragraphs: Watch for changes that require professional advice, including worsening pain, swelling or other signs of possible infection. Follow clinician directions for wound care.
Detailed bleeding control, dressing methods and infection advice should be reviewed by a qualified first-aid or healthcare professional before publication.

articles.title: Leak or burst pipe at home
articles.summary: Protect people, document problems and contact the right water or property service.

sections.title: Locate the problem safely
paragraphs: Water leaks can affect floor surfaces, ceilings, shared flats and electrical installations. Distinguish a dripping fitting from a significant leak only to the extent it is safe to observe.
Do not enter areas where water may be in contact with damaged electrical systems or unstable building materials.

sections.title: Who is responsible
paragraphs: Keep the details for your water supplier, landlord, managing agent, building emergency contact and plumber in the household plan.
The responsible party depends on whether the issue is inside your home, part of shared building infrastructure or on the supply network.

sections.title: Record and recover
paragraphs: Document what you observed and the time of the problem, without risking injury. Use qualified tradespeople for repairs where appropriate.
After a serious leak, some electrical and building components may require professional assessment before use.

articles.title: Food during a power cut
articles.summary: Why food-safety decisions depend on time, temperature and the type of product.

sections.title: Understand food storage risk
paragraphs: Refrigerated and frozen foods can become unsafe when storage temperatures are not maintained. The type of food, actual temperature and time outside recommended conditions matter.
An app cannot determine whether a particular item is safe to eat from its barcode or the time of a power cut alone.

sections.title: Prepare beforehand
paragraphs: Keep an inventory of foods, storage locations and dates. Know which items are shelf-stable and which rely on refrigeration.
Record food-safety advice from your applicable national authority as part of the reviewed guide release; do not invent universal safe-hour thresholds.

sections.title: After service returns
paragraphs: Review affected foods using official criteria that apply to your situation. When uncertain about safety, seek authoritative advice rather than relying on appearance or smell alone.
This article is an editorial draft pending review against Food Standards Agency and Food Standards Scotland guidance.

articles.title: Unsafe or contaminated water
articles.summary: Understand different water quality notices and why the precise wording matters.

sections.title: Different notices mean different things
paragraphs: An interruption in water supply differs from a water quality warning. Boil-water, do-not-drink and do-not-use notices can require different responses.
Treat the current notice from the water company or public-health authority as the relevant instruction. This article cannot verify water safety.

sections.title: Make a household plan
paragraphs: Record your water provider contact and plan for anyone requiring water for feeding, personal care or medical equipment.
Inventory records can help identify stored drinking-water supplies, but they do not assess packaging integrity or actual water quality.

sections.title: When notices change
paragraphs: Use official communications for changes to restrictions and restoration. Do not assume that normal pressure or clear-looking water proves that a warning has ended.
Detailed treatment procedures require qualified public-health review.

articles.title: Contacting family without internet
articles.summary: Simple arrangements when mobile data, broadband or online messaging are unavailable.

sections.title: Plan ahead
paragraphs: Agree how household members will communicate during service disruption and where they will look for official information. Write key contact numbers in a place accessible without unlocking a phone.
Decide who will check on people who may need assistance and how to avoid everyone independently travelling to the same location.

sections.title: Choose practical backups
paragraphs: A charged phone, power bank, paper contact sheet and battery-powered radio may be useful. Test equipment occasionally rather than relying solely on inventory counts.
Some communication services require electricity or network connectivity; no method can be guaranteed during every emergency.

sections.title: Review after a disruption
paragraphs: Update stale contact details and revise any meeting arrangement that proved impractical. Avoid storing private household details inside the public reference library.
This is a general planning article and should be adapted to the needs and accessibility of each household.

articles.title: Check and maintain a torch
articles.summary: Routine preparedness inspection for lighting equipment stored at home.

sections.title: Find and inspect the item
paragraphs: Know which household storage location contains your torch or emergency light. Look for visible damage, corrosion or missing parts before relying on it.
A torch marked available in inventory might not work, so periodic physical checks are important.

sections.title: Check the power source
paragraphs: Confirm that the torch works according to its manufacturer's instructions and that compatible batteries or charging accessories are available.
Do not use swollen, damaged, leaking or overheating rechargeable batteries; follow manufacturer and local waste-disposal guidance.

sections.title: Record the result
paragraphs: Mark the inspection date in your household plan and identify any replacement needed. Keep a suitable light accessible to people likely to need it.
This is a low-complexity draft; product-specific maintenance instructions should still come from the equipment manufacturer.
